newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. vetoes Boutros-Ghali; 14 other states approve.
newsitem.headline: U.S. vetoes Boutros-Ghali; 14 other states approve.

text.p: The United States on Tuesday vetoed a second term for Boutros Boutros-Ghali as secretary-general of the United Nations, standing alone against all other 14 members of the Security Council.
Despite the veto, there were no signs Boutros-Ghali would withdraw in favour of another African candidate, creating a deadlock between Washington and his supporters.

"He's in this until the Security Council makes a final decision," U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa said. In an obvious reference to the United States, she said the 14-1 vote should be noted by "member states,"
Boutros-Ghali himself told Fox News that he had to respect the U.S. position because "without the cooperation of the United States, I will not be able to fulfil my job."
"I still hope we may have a change of attitude of certain members," he said in an apparent reference to Washington.

The council has agreed to give priority to candidates from Africa on the grounds that if Boutros-Ghali is denied the second term given his predecessors, he should at least be followed by another African.

Delegates from 52 African states met to sort out their next move but decided to refer the issue back to their capitals and the Organisation of African Unity, which had supported Boutros-Ghali. Members attending the meeting told Reuters that most members were determined to keep submitting Boutros-Ghali's name "over and over again."

In 1981, for example, then-Secretary-General Kurt Waldheim of Austria was vetoed repeatedly by China while the United States opposed Salim A. Salim of Tanzania. Both candidates withdrew after 15 ballots and the council chose Peruvian Javier Perez de Cuellar.
The current council president, Nugroho Wisnumurti of Indonesia, said he was opening the list to African candidates, adding that "we should maintain the momentum."
U.S. ambassador Madeleine Albright made it clear that there would be no change of position, saying she had "standing instructions" to veto Boutros-Ghali's candidacy.

In Ottawa, Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy expressed disappointment with Washington's veto and told reporters: "We just hope that this...doesn't impair or hinder the work the U.N. is doing in Zaire and Haiti."

Washington found itself isolated after first announcing its opposition to Boutros-Ghali last June in The New York Times and because it has failed to pay $1.4 billion in debts to the United Nations, bankrupting the world body.

U.S. officials have argued that Boutros-Ghali has not taken enough initiatives to streamline the world body and that replacing him is the only way to persuade the Republican-controlled Congress to come up with the funds.

In Washington, State Department spokesman Glyn Davies said, "At the end of the day, the United Nations needs the United States more than -- with all due respect -- it needs to retain its current leadership. We think that what's important today is preserving U.N. status as the premier international organisation. "
"We're an immovable object on Boutros-Ghali and you saw the concrete manifestation of that in our veto in New York today," he added.

After Tuesday's vote, Wisnumurti said that the ballots were marked to distinguish the council's five permanent members with veto power -- the United States, Britain, France, Russia and China -- from the 10 non-permanent members.
The 14 states for Boutros-Ghali were France, Britain, Russia, China, Botswana, Chile, Egypt, Germany, Guinea-Bissau, Honduras, Indonesia, Italy, South Korea and Poland.
Four of them -- Britain, Italy, South Korea and Poland -- did not sponsor the resolution, indicating they might be willing to move on to another candidate.

Among Africans mentioned as potential candidates are Under-Secretary-General Kofi Annan of Ghana, who heads U.N. peacekeeping operations; Hamid Algabid of Niger, secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference; and Salim A. Salim of Tanzania, the secretary-general of the Organisation of African Unity.
